name: Pap (Ogi/Akamu) with Akara
summary: Smooth, tangy fermented corn porridge served with crisp, spicy black-eyed pea fritters.
story: Ogi (Yoruba) or akamu (Igbo) is a fermented cereal porridge that is a classic Nigerian breakfast, and is also given to babies and the unwell. Pairing it with fried akara bean fritters is a beloved morning combination.

items.name: ogi (fermented corn starch)
items.note: ready-made, or see steps for homemade

steps.title: Prepare the beans
steps.text: Soak the peas in cold water for about 1 hour, then rub them between your palms in water until the skins float off. Pour off the skins and rinse until the beans are white and clean.

steps.title: Blend the batter
steps.text: Blend the peeled beans with the onion and pepper using as little water as you can, until a thick, fluffy paste forms. It should hold on a spoon and not run.

steps.title: Beat the batter
steps.text: Add the salt and beat vigorously with a wooden spoon for 3-4 minutes. The batter turns pale and airy, which makes the akara light.

steps.title: Fry the akara
steps.text: Heat the oil to about 180 C (350 F). Scoop spoonfuls of batter into the oil and fry for 3-4 minutes, turning, until deep golden and crisp. Drain on paper towels.

steps.title: Mix the ogi
steps.text: Stir the ogi with the cold water in a bowl until completely smooth with no lumps. Have the boiling water ready.

steps.title: Cook the pap
steps.text: Pour the boiling water onto the ogi in a thin stream while stirring fast. It will thicken and turn translucent and glossy. If it stays pale and thin, return it to low heat and stir for 2-3 minutes.

steps.title: Serve hot
steps.text: Spoon into bowls, sweeten and add milk if you like, and serve alongside the hot akara.

tips: Add boiling water gradually and stir continuously or lumps form.
Beans must be dry-ish and well beaten for fluffy akara; too much water makes it flat and oily.
Wet your spoon for scooping batter so it releases cleanly.
Pap thickens as it cools, so loosen with hot water if needed.

swaps.swap: Fine cornmeal or custard-style corn starch gives a similar texture, but lacks the tangy fermented taste.
Peeled brown beans are common in Nigeria; dried skinless black-eyed peas from African shops save the peeling step.
